newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugoslavia T-bill sale seen keeping govt pledge.
newsitem.headline: Yugoslavia T-bill sale seen keeping govt pledge.

text.p: Yugoslavia will put on sale for the first time next week 100 million dinars (17.6 million) worth of Treasury bills and analysts say the state looks set to keep a promise not to tap the central bank for its needs.

"This is a new way for the government to raise funds for its budget needs because it does not seek direct help from the central bank. Even more important is that the state debt becomes more transparent," a market analyst said on Tuesday.
The government said earlier it would raise a total of 100 million dinars via 30-day and 60-day T-bills to finance the army's liabilities with commercial suppliers.
Yugoslavia's 1997 budget is determined at 9.238 billion dinars, 6.5 billion of which is earmarked for defence.
T-bills, issued at 500, 1,000 and 10,000 dinars face value, can be bought by companies at the local bourse and individuals through licenced banks and used for paying customs and other import duties.
Gordana Dostanic, head of the trading floor at the Belgrade bourse, said T-bills will be put on sale under pre-determined conditions, with precise interest rates.
"There will be no competition among bidders. The government has already made all conditions clear. All orders will be handed over to a bourse broker," Dostanic told Reuters.
"The government will sell only 100 million dinars worth of T-bills. In case of demand exceeding supply, lucky buyers will be taken out of a hat. But that's unlikely to happen," she said.
T-bills, issued in two tranches of 50 million dinars each, carry a 4.5 percent monthly interest.
Tranche "A" of 30-day T-bills matures on June 11 and can be used to pay customs duties 20 days after the purchasing date.
Another tranche "B" of 60-day T-bills matures on July 11 and the paper can be used to pay customs duties 30 days after purchasing date.
Holders of T-bills will be able to pay customs and other import duties with the T-bill face value increased by interest written on the back of the paper.
Dostanic said T-bills were more attractive for domestic than foreign investors because they carried some customs relief,
"We expect mainly forwarding companies and big importers to buy the paper but banks may also appear as buyers," she said.
"This is a risk-free investment and both the principal and the interest are paid back from the state budget," she added.
The interest rate, lower than on other commercial investment on the bourse running as high as 12 percent per month, results from the low risk.
Dostanic expected T-bills to become a subject of secondary trading.

"T-bills can easily become attractive. There is always a great interest but monetary authorities can make the paper even more attractive if they offer to banks a possibility to use bills from their portfolio for liquidity purposes," she said.
The central bank is expected to detail other benefits for investors, particularly to commercial banks, the bourse said in a news release.
Ljiljana Stanisic, assistant to the finance minister in charge of budget issues, said foreigners by law were allowed to buy T-bills.
"Any foreigner with established legal status in Yugoslavia can buy T-bills. But they will not enjoy any more privileges than domestic investors," Stanisic said.
Government officials said it was too early to say whether the state would go for another T-bill issue by end-1997.
"It all depends on how successful this issue will be," said a government official who asked not to be named. -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
